alignment.note: Greek κατηγόρουν and Latin accusabant both render the imperfect 'were accusing' with a single verb; the Peshitta employs the idiomatic compound ܐܟܠ ܩܪܨܐ (literally 'to eat the pieces/morsels of'), a fixed Syriac expression for slanderous accusation, periphrastically reinforced by the auxiliary ܗܘܘ to express durative past aspect.

Greek marks the object with the genitive αὐτοῦ governed by κατηγορέω, and Latin uses accusative eum; in the Peshitta the pronominal suffix -ܘܗܝ is fused directly onto the idiomatic noun ܩܪܨܘܗܝ ('his pieces'), so the object pronoun is morphologically incorporated rather than standing as a discrete word.

Greek ἀρχιερεῖς ('chief priests') is rendered analytically in both versions as a construct phrase 'great/chief ones of the priests' (Syriac ܪܒܝ ܟܗܢܐ, Latin summi sacerdotes), reflecting the absence of a single composite lexeme in Syriac and Latin for the Greek compound noun.

Greek uses the bare adverbial accusative neuter plural πολλά ('of many things'); the Peshitta renders this with a prepositional phrase ܒܣܓܝܐܬܐ ('in/with many things'), and the Vulgate likewise expands to the prepositional in multis, both supplying an explicit preposition where Greek relies on the adverbial accusative alone.
